title: Animal Migration
keyIdea: Migration is a long trip an animal makes, and then it comes back. Animals travel to find food, to have babies, or to follow the seasons. Arctic terns fly pole to pole, monarch butterflies spend winter in Mexico, wildebeest follow rain around the Serengeti for fresh grass, and humpback whales feed in cold seas then swim to warm seas to have calves. Hibernation is staying put, not migration.
familyTip: When you see swallows gather in autumn, or a nature programme about whales or wildebeest, ask: is this animal leaving for good, or will it come back? What is it looking for — food, a place to have babies, or a better season? Compare that with a hedgehog curled up in a nest: it is still at home.

visual.caption: Does each animal migrate (a long trip and back) or stay nearby? Drag each card, or tap it then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: fly a tern pole to pole and back, match routes and reasons, see why whales use warm seas, and sort migration from staying or hibernating.

kid: Migration is a long trip an animal makes, and then it comes back. Animals do not wander or get lost. They travel to find food, to have babies, or to follow the seasons.
Arctic terns fly from the far north to the far south and back. That is the longest migration. Monarch butterflies fly thousands of miles to Mexico for the winter.
Wildebeest walk around the Serengeti following the rain, so they can eat fresh grass. Humpback whales feed in cold seas, then swim to warm seas to have their calves.
Not every animal migrates. A garden snail stays near home. A hedgehog sleeps through winter in its nest. That is hibernation, not migration.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. Primary science looks at habitats and how seasons change what animals need. Migration is a long trip, usually each year, for food, breeding or climate. The animal comes back. For monarch butterflies, later generations complete the return.

Arctic terns breed in the Arctic and spend the other summer near the Antarctic. Tracking studies show about 70,000 to 90,000 km a year. Eastern North American monarchs spend winter in fir forests in central Mexico. The butterflies that fly south do not finish the whole loop north. Their young keep going. Wildebeest follow rain and fresh grass around the Serengeti and the Mara. Humpback whales feed on krill and small fish in cold seas. They swim to warmer water to have calves, and they eat little there.

Common mistakes: thinking the animal leaves for good (that would be a one-way move, not a migration). Thinking whales go to the tropics to feed, when the food is in the cold seas. Mixing up who goes where (monarchs do not fly pole to pole; that is the tern). Calling hibernation migration, because both happen in winter. A hedgehog sleeping in its nest stays put.

In the lab your child flies an Arctic tern from north to south and back, so they see a round trip. They match each animal to its route and its reason, then face the whale trap (warm seas are for calves, not krill). They sort animals that migrate from ones that stay, including a hibernating hedgehog.

choices: a long trip an animal makes, and then it comes back
any time an animal walks to a new home and stays there
sleeping through winter in a nest
practice.hint: Think about whether the animal returns, and why it went.
practice.explain: Migration is a long trip for food, babies or the seasons, and then a return. Moving house for good is not migration. Sleeping in a nest all winter is hibernation.

practice.prompt: Which animal flies from the far north to the far south and back?
choices: Arctic tern
monarch butterfly
wildebeest
practice.hint: One of these makes the longest migration, pole to pole.
practice.explain: The Arctic tern flies pole to pole and back. Monarchs fly to Mexico for winter. Wildebeest walk a loop around the Serengeti following the rain.

practice.prompt: {a} Arctic terns and {b} monarch butterflies migrate. {c} garden snails stay near home. How many of these animals migrate?
practice.hint: Count only the animals that make a long trip and come back. Snails stay near home.
practice.explain: Terns and monarchs migrate, so {a} + {b} = {=a+b}. The {c} snails stay, so they are not counted.

practice.prompt: An Arctic tern flies south and back north each year. In {n} years, how many one-way flights between the poles does it make?
practice.hint: Each year the tern flies south once and north once.
practice.explain: Each year has 2 one-way flights. In {n} years that is 2 × {n} = {=2*n}.

practice.prompt: Humpback whales swim to warm seas mainly to…
choices: have their calves
feed on more krill
roost in fir trees
practice.hint: Think about where the whale's food lives, and what a newborn calf needs.
practice.explain: The food (krill and small fish) is in cold seas. Whales swim to warm seas to have calves, and they eat little there. Monarchs, not whales, roost in trees.

pool.prompt: Wildebeest walk around the Serengeti following the rain so they can…
choices: eat fresh grass
fly to Mexico
sleep in a nest all winter
pool.hint: Their loop tracks where new grass grows after rain.
pool.explain: Wildebeest migrate for food: they follow rainfall and graze fresh grass. They do not fly, and they do not hibernate.

pool.prompt: A hedgehog sleeps through winter in its nest. Is that migration?
choices: No, it stays put: that is hibernation
Yes, because it is a winter change
Yes, any long rest is a migration
pool.hint: Does the hedgehog make a long trip, or does it stay in its nest?
pool.explain: Hibernation means staying put and sleeping through winter. Migration means a long trip and a return. The hedgehog does not travel.

pool.prompt: Monarch butterflies fly thousands of miles in autumn to…
choices: spend winter in Mexico
swim to the Antarctic
hunt wildebeest
pool.hint: These butterflies roost in forests much farther south, but not at a pole.
pool.explain: Eastern North American monarchs fly to central Mexico for winter. Pole-to-pole flight is the Arctic tern. Wildebeest are grazers, not butterfly prey.

pool.prompt: Where do humpback whales do most of their feeding?
choices: in cold seas, on krill and small fish
in warm seas, while the calf is born
in Mexico, in fir trees
pool.hint: The big meal and the calf are not in the same place.
pool.explain: Food is plentiful in cold, high-latitude waters. Warm seas are for calving. Fir trees are a monarch winter roost, not a whale habitat.

pool.prompt: {a} humpback whales swim to warm seas to have calves. {b} garden snails stay near home. How many of these animals are migrating?
pool.hint: Only count the animals making a long trip they will return from.
pool.explain: The {a} whales are migrating. The {b} snails stay, so the number that migrate is {a}.

pool.prompt: A researcher watches {t} Arctic terns and {w} wildebeest migrate, and {s} hedgehogs hibernate. How many of these animals migrate?
pool.hint: Hibernating animals stay in their nests, so they do not migrate.
pool.explain: Terns and wildebeest migrate: {t} + {w} = {=t+w}. The {s} hedgehogs hibernate, so they are not counted.

pool.prompt: An Arctic tern flies south and stays there. A friend says that is migration. What is missing?
choices: the return: migration is a round trip
nothing: any long flight is migration
it should have walked, not flown
pool.hint: Migration is not just going away. Think about what happens next.
pool.explain: If the bird left for good, that would be a one-way move. Migration includes coming back (or, for monarchs, later generations continuing the loop).

choices: Arctic tern: pole to pole; monarch: Mexico for winter
monarch: pole to pole; wildebeest: Mexico for winter
humpback whale: Mexico for winter; tern: Serengeti grass
pool.hint: Keep each animal with its own route.
pool.explain: Terns fly pole to pole. Monarchs spend winter in Mexico. Wildebeest follow rain around the Serengeti. Whales move from cold feeding seas to warm calving seas.
